theory.heading: Begin with three personal themes
theory.body: A personal emblem communicates something about you through a small, recognisable design. Begin by listing three different themes that matter to you. These might come from your initials, a place, a hobby, an animal or a significant number. Choose themes with a clear personal connection rather than selecting an image only because it looks impressive. Briefly explain what each theme means to you. Starting with three themes creates choice and helps prevent the first idea from becoming the final design without comparison.

theory.heading: Gather and study references
theory.body: Collect several visual references for each theme. References can help you notice common outlines, shapes, patterns and symbols. Study them to understand how an idea can be communicated simply. Look for features that make the subject recognisable, such as the curve of an animal, the outline of a landscape or the arrangement of initials. Record where each idea came from and describe what you learned. Research should support your thinking, not provide a finished emblem to copy.

theory.heading: Turn meaning into simple shapes
theory.body: Select useful features from your research and translate them into your own simple shapes. Remove details that do not help communicate the main idea. Consider whether a viewer could recognise the theme and whether the design meaning matches your intention. Combining or changing reference features can help create an original response. Avoid tracing or slightly altering a completed emblem because that does not show your own design thinking. Current school SOPs and teacher directions control all actual workshop activity. If a reference or design choice is uncertain, ask before continuing.

questions.question: How many personal themes should a student begin with?
choices: Three
Two
One
Five
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Beginning with three themes creates useful choice before developing a design.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Begin with three personal themes and focus on the recommended starting number.

questions.question: Which option is a suitable source for a personal theme?
choices: The first finished logo found online
A meaningful hobby
A random image with no connection
Another student's final emblem
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A meaningful hobby can provide a clear personal connection for an emblem.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Begin with three personal themes and identify the types of personal ideas suggested.

questions.question: Why should a student briefly explain each theme?
choices: To make every theme look identical
To avoid gathering references
To show its personal meaning
To select a finished emblem immediately
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Explaining each theme clarifies why it matters and what it could communicate.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Begin with three personal themes and focus on what should be recorded about each theme.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of gathering visual references?
choices: To copy a finished emblem exactly
To avoid making design decisions
To prove one theme is always best
To notice useful shapes, outlines and symbols
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. References help students identify visual features that communicate an idea.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Gather and study references and focus on what students should notice in the examples.

questions.question: Which observation would be useful when studying an animal reference?
choices: The price of the image
The outline that makes the animal recognisable
The number of colours on the webpage
The name of another student's design
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A recognisable outline can help communicate the animal using simple shapes.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Gather and study references and identify the kinds of visual features worth studying.

questions.question: How should research support emblem design?
choices: By providing a finished design to trace
By replacing personal meaning
By helping the student understand and develop ideas
By forcing all students to use the same symbol
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Research should inform original thinking rather than replace it.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Gather and study references and focus on the final sentence about the role of research.

questions.question: What should a student do with details that do not support the main idea?
choices: Add more of them
Make them the largest feature
Copy them from another emblem
Remove or simplify them
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Removing unnecessary detail helps the emblem communicate its main idea clearly.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Turn meaning into simple shapes and focus on how unnecessary details should be handled.

questions.question: Which approach best supports an original emblem?
choices: Combining and adapting useful reference features
Changing only one tiny detail
Tracing a completed emblem
Copying another student's layout
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Combining and adapting reference features shows independent design thinking.
questions.retryFeedback: Return to Turn meaning into simple shapes and identify how references can be transformed into an original response.

questions.question: What should a student check when reviewing a developing emblem?
choices: Whether it uses the most details possible
Whether it matches a commercial logo
Whether the theme is recognisable and the meaning is clear
Whether another student prefers it
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. A useful review checks recognisability and whether the design communicates the intended meaning.
questions.retryFeedback: Re-read Turn meaning into simple shapes and focus on the questions used to judge the design.

questions.question: Why should a student avoid copying a finished emblem?
choices: It prevents the use of simple shapes
It guarantees the theme will be unclear
It makes research unnecessary
It does not demonstrate original design thinking
questions.correctFeedback: Correct. Copying a finished emblem does not show the student's own research and design decisions.
questions.retryFeedback: Review Turn meaning into simple shapes and identify why tracing or slightly altering a completed design should be avoided.

written.prompt: Identify three possible personal themes for an emblem, explain the meaning of each and describe one simple visual feature that could represent each theme without copying a finished design.
written.sentenceStarter: My three themes are ___, ___ and ___. They matter to me because ___. A simple feature I could explore for each is ___.
written.example: My three themes are my initials, fishing and the local river. They connect to my identity, interests and place. I could explore joined letter shapes, a simple fish outline and a curved line representing the river.
